_about: Course structure for scripts/site_sync.py. Lesson ids, titles and minutes come from assets/js/course-data.js; this file only adds what that file lacks: each chapter's navbar label and Font Awesome icon, and the one-line lesson summaries shown on chapter pages (HTML allowed).

blurbs.1-1: What a robot is, where the word came from, and the sense, think, act loop every robot shares.
blurbs.1-2: How automation evolved over time, from early attempts at automatic machines to modern automation.
blurbs.1-3: The main types of robots: industrial arms, cobots, mobile robots, SCARA robots and autonomous guided vehicles.
blurbs.1-4: The skills worth having before starting robotics: Python, C++, some math, the right learning mentality, assembly language and networking basics.
blurbs.1-5: Where robots are used: in production, in interaction with people, in scientific exploration and in protecting human lives.
blurbs.1-6: How an industrial arm is built: joints, degrees of freedom, the work envelope, coordinate frames, the tool center point, and how a controller interpolates joint and straight-line moves.
blurbs.1-7: What turns a robot arm into a working cell: components, safeguarding and light-curtain distance, PLC-robot handshakes, integrator roles with FAT and SAT, three typical cells, cycle time and cost.

blurbs.2-1: The two ways industrial robots are programmed: offline in simulation software, and online with a teach pendant or by hand guiding.
blurbs.2-2: Two widely used robot programming environments: ABB RobotStudio for offline programming and simulation, and Universal Robots PolyScope for cobots.
blurbs.2-3: Industrial robot languages: Universal Robots' URScript, ABB's RAPID, and RRL.
blurbs.2-4: Why ROS exists: a common, vendor-agnostic layer for programming robots from different makers.
blurbs.2-5: How to choose and size grippers, mount them and set payload, and program the digital I/O that opens a gripper, confirms a grip and talks to a PLC, in URScript and RAPID.
blurbs.2-6: Build a complete pick-and-place cycle in URSim (and RobotStudio): TCP and payload, a three-point fixture frame, approach offsets, exact stops at the grip, and re-teaching only three points when the fixture moves.
blurbs.2-7: How robot programs are organized (RAPID modules and routines, URScript functions and threads) and how they recover from errors such as a missed pick, with a 3 by 3 palletizing loop.
blurbs.2-8: How robots use cameras to pick parts that are not in a fixed place: 2D versus 3D guidance, camera mounting, lens and hand-eye calibration, and the frame-shift math that turns a vision result into a correct pick.

blurbs.3-1: What open source is: licenses, public artifacts, core repository files (README, CONTRIBUTING, CODE_OF_CONDUCT, LICENSE), and ROS 2 package examples.
blurbs.3-2: Finding your first contribution: non-code tasks, beginner labels, the fork and pull request workflow, and public communication norms.
blurbs.3-3: How robotics projects work: ROS 2 rolling development, backport rules, DCO sign-off, build farm testing, and governance across MoveIt 2, ros2_control, Gazebo, and Nav2.
blurbs.3-4: Lab: making your first pull request to robOSStics by fixing a typo or broken source in the browser or locally with verification checks.

blurbs.4-1: What ROS is and how it splits a robot into nodes that communicate by publishing and subscribing to messages.
blurbs.4-2: The history of ROS and the main differences between ROS 1 and ROS 2: communication protocol, launch files, and compatibility and flexibility.
blurbs.4-3: How to install ROS on Windows (x86-64 and ARM), macOS (ARM) and Linux (x86).
blurbs.4-4: A first hands-on ROS example using the Turtlesim simulator.
blurbs.4-5: The ROS tools you will use most: RViz, Gazebo and popular ROS packages.
blurbs.4-6: Build a ROS 2 Lyrical Python package from scratch: workspaces and overlays, ros2 pkg create, setup.py and package.xml, rosdep, colcon, and a timer-driven node that drives Turtlesim in a square.
blurbs.4-7: Start many ROS 2 nodes with one command: Python and XML launch files, namespaces, remapping, launch arguments, and YAML parameter files on Lyrical Luth.
blurbs.4-8: Plan and execute arm motions with MoveIt 2 on ROS 2 Lyrical: URDF and SRDF, ros2_control mock hardware, move_group, OMPL and Pilz PTP/LIN, and a UR5e in RViz.
blurbs.4-9: How ROS 2 drives real industrial arms: ROS-Industrial, the common driver pattern, and the UR, ABB, FANUC, KUKA and Yaskawa drivers, with real-time and safety limits.

blurbs.5-2: The ethical questions robots raise, and the safety layer every robot needs in hardware and software.
blurbs.5-3: The social questions robots raise beyond safety: jobs and automation, privacy from robot sensors, and accountability for autonomous decisions.
blurbs.5-4: A practical integrator workflow for robot cell safety: the ISO 12100 three-step method, task-based risk assessment, guards and safety distances, performance levels, robot safety functions and lockout/tagout.
blurbs.5-5: Where AI is really used in industrial robotics as of October 2026 (learned vision, predictive maintenance, LLM coding assistants, research foundation models), what the evidence says about AI-written code, and how to check it before it moves a real arm.

blurbs.6-1: The Arduino basics a robot programmer needs: pin types, the setup and loop structure, driving servos and DC motors, reading sensors and debugging.
blurbs.6-2: How PWM lets a digital pin control motor speed, servo angle and LED brightness, and the practical details that matter on a real robot.
blurbs.6-3: How encoders let a robot measure how far and how fast its motors have turned: incremental vs. absolute, quadrature, the math, and common pitfalls.
blurbs.6-4: How a PID controller uses sensor feedback to move a robot smoothly and precisely: the three terms, a code example, tuning, and common pitfalls.
blurbs.6-5: The sensors small robots use most: ultrasonic range finders, IMUs, color and line sensors, and cameras, and what each can and cannot measure.
blurbs.6-6: How a wheeled robot estimates its position from wheel encoders, the equations for a differential drive, and why the estimate drifts.
blurbs.6-7: How to organize robot behavior as states and transitions, with a worked example and Arduino code that never blocks.
blurbs.6-8: Why robots fuse sensors, and how a one-dimensional Kalman filter blends a prediction with a noisy measurement.
blurbs.6-9: How robots turn a target into smooth setpoints: trapezoidal, triangular and S-curve profiles, cubic and quintic time scaling, joint, linear and circular interpolation, zones, and time parameterization in MoveIt.
blurbs.6-10: The full math of a planar two-link arm: forward kinematics, the reachable ring, closed-form inverse kinematics with atan2, rounding edge cases, and the Jacobian singularity.

blurbs.7-1: Industrial camera sensors and optics: CMOS versus CCD, global and rolling shutters, pixel size and Nyquist resolution, focal length and f-number, telecentric lenses, and GenICam.
blurbs.7-2: Illumination for machine vision: backlighting, ring, glancing, darkfield, diffuse dome, coaxial and in-line lighting, optical filters, cross-polarization, and LED strobing.
blurbs.7-3: Core 2D image processing: color space conversion, histograms and contrast equalization, global, Otsu and adaptive thresholding, contours, moments, blobs, Canny edge detection, and template matching.
blurbs.7-4: 3D perception for robotics: direct sensing versus 2D inference, stereo disparity geometry, point cloud filtering with PCL (PassThrough, VoxelGrid, outliers), RANSAC planes, Euclidean clustering, and bin picking.
blurbs.7-5: Automated inspection and measurement: optical resolution and the Nyquist limit, telecentric gauging, lens distortion calibration, presence verification, and 1D/2D barcode quality.
blurbs.7-6: Build a ROS 2 camera pipeline in Python: sensor_msgs/Image and CameraInfo, optical frames, image_transport, cv_bridge conversion, and real-time OpenCV edge processing; runs without a camera using cam2image test images.

blurbs.8-1: From discrete wiring to industrial networks: sinking and sourcing (NPN/PNP), fieldbus history, line, star and ring topologies, cyclic versus acyclic data, and Device Level Ring recovery.
blurbs.8-2: Industrial Ethernet protocols: EtherNet/IP CIP implicit and explicit messaging, PROFINET RT and IRT with GSDML, EtherCAT on-the-fly frame processing with ESI, and Modbus TCP.
blurbs.8-3: Lab: the UR Modbus TCP server and its general-purpose registers, packing handshake bits in URScript, and writing and reading registers from Python with pymodbus (stand-in server, no hardware).
blurbs.8-4: Functional safety over industrial networks: the black channel principle, PROFIsafe, FailSafe over EtherCAT (FSoE), CIP Safety, and stop category classifications.
blurbs.8-5: Integrating plant-floor devices with enterprise IT: IO-Link sensor architecture, OPC UA information modeling and the VDMA 40010 robotics specification, MQTT telemetry, and ros2_control.
blurbs.8-6: Network design, security and diagnostics: ISA/IEC 62443, zones and the DMZ, VLANs, Time-Sensitive Networking, and a Wireshark lab that decodes the 8.3 Modbus traffic.

blurbs.9-1: Preventive, predictive and reactive maintenance strategies: inspection intervals, cleaning and ESD protection, fastener torque checks, and maintenance records.
blurbs.9-2: A systematic troubleshooting method: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147 lockout/tagout, controller error logs, flight records, and avoiding masked faults.
blurbs.9-3: Mechanical fault diagnosis: cable dress packs and carriers, bend radii, seal inspection, collision recovery in backdrive mode, and joint brake engagement.
blurbs.9-4: Electrical and I/O troubleshooting: multimeter voltage and continuity checks, discrete sensor wiring, 24 V power budgets, and fieldbus diagnostics.
blurbs.9-5: Calibration, backups and recovery: axis revolution counter updates, TCP calibration, joint replacement alignment, and controller storage backups.
blurbs.9-6: Lab: querying the Universal Robots Dashboard Server over TCP port 29999 with Python to check robot mode, safety status, and recover from protective stops.

blurbs.10-1: Capstone project: build a simulated pick-and-place work cell in URSim or ABB RobotStudio with gripper I/O, a safety configuration and a FAT-style test sheet, graded by milestones and a four-level rubric.
blurbs.10-2: Capstone project: build a pick-and-place task for a simulated UR5e with ROS 2, MoveIt 2 and the MoveIt Task Constructor on mock hardware or Gazebo, with milestones, tests and a rubric.
blurbs.10-3: Capstone project: build an Arduino speed-controlled wheel with a quadrature encoder, H-bridge driver, PID loop and a state machine with ramps and a FAULT state, with milestones, safety and a rubric.
blurbs.10-4: Capstone project: an open-source ROS 2 cell monitor that reads robot state, packed Modbus handshake bits and a camera check from stand-in servers, keeps a maintenance log, and ends with a real pull request. No hardware needed.
